issues: Summary says Public Law 91-508 was 'a statute whose earlier titles imposed record-keeping and currency-reporting duties on banks'. Only Titles I (Financial Recordkeeping) and II (Reports of Currency and Foreign Transactions) do. Title III covers margin requirements, Title IV effective dates and Title V credit cards (checked in the govinfo scan). Title II also applies to financial institutions beyond banks.

Significance overstates the 1970 access right. The original § 609 required a bureau to disclose 'the nature and substance of all information (except medical information)' in its files, in person or by telephone (§ 610). It did not require letting the consumer see or copy the file. 'Restrict' also misattributes agency: the Act itself limited who could obtain reports (§ 604 permissible purposes), not the consumer.

Significance says 'The first US law aimed at a private data industry' with no source. EPIC supports the narrower wording: 'the first federal law to regulate the use of personal information by private businesses'. EPIC is added as a source.

Other claims confirmed: 'Approved October 26, 1970' printed at the end of P.L. 91-508; § 602(a)(4) quote verbatim; § 602(b) 'confidentiality, accuracy, relevancy, and proper utilization'; Title VI effective 180 days after enactment; FTC enforcement (the FTC page notes the Commission 'retains all its enforcement authority').

fieldFixes.summary: The Fair Credit Reporting Act was approved on 26 October 1970 as Title VI of Public Law 91-508, a statute whose Titles I and II imposed record-keeping and currency-reporting duties on banks and other financial institutions. It found a need to ensure that consumer reporting agencies act with 'a respect for the consumer's right to privacy', required them to adopt reasonable procedures for the confidentiality, accuracy, relevancy and proper use of information, and limited disclosure of consumer reports to purposes specified in the Act. On request, a bureau had to tell consumers 'the nature and substance' of the information it held on them. The Federal Trade Commission enforces it.
fieldFixes.significance: The first federal law to regulate private businesses' use of personal information, it gave people a right to learn what a credit bureau's file on them said and to dispute it, and restricted who could obtain it.

issues: Misattributed quote subject. The summary says the report concluded that 'intelligence agencies' had 'undermined the constitutional rights of citizens'. The report itself (Book II, S. Rep. 94-755) reads: 'The Committee's fundamental conclusion is that intelligence activities have undermined the constitutional rights of citizens and that they have done so primarily because checks and balances ... have not been applied.' The Senate Historical Office page, the only source on the record, paraphrases this as 'Intelligence agencies have undermined...' inside quotation marks.

'Made 96 recommendations' is incomplete. The 96 numbered recommendations are in Book II (Intelligence Activities and the Rights of Americans); Recommendation 96 is the last in Book II. Book I (Foreign and Military Intelligence) contains its own numbered recommendations running to 87. The final report as a whole therefore made more than 96.

End date: the Senate Historical Office gives 'Final report issued: Apr 29, 1976', but Books I and II are both dated 'APRIL 26 (legislative day, APRIL 14), 1976' on their title pages. The public release date could not be confirmed independently, so the end date is best given as April 1976 with the 26 April report date in the summary.
Confirmed: resolution passed 27 January 1975 (82-4); SHAMROCK and MINARET 'monitored wire communications to and from the United States'; COINTELPRO investigated.

fieldFixes.summary: The Senate created the Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities, chaired by Senator Frank Church, by a resolution passed on 27 January 1975. Its investigators uncovered the NSA's SHAMROCK and MINARET programmes, which monitored wire communications to and from the United States, and documented the FBI's COINTELPRO. In its final report, dated 26 April 1976, the committee stated its 'fundamental conclusion' that intelligence activities had 'undermined the constitutional rights of citizens'. The report's volume on domestic intelligence made 96 recommendations, and its volume on foreign and military intelligence 87 more.

fieldFixes.summary: The first version of the Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG), titled 'Gesetz zum Schutz vor Missbrauch personenbezogener Daten bei der Datenverarbeitung', was enacted on 27 January 1977, the date the statute bears (BGBl. I 1977 S. 201). It made processing of personal data lawful only with the data subject's consent or where the act or another legal provision permitted it, and covered companies as well as public bodies. The act established a Federal Data Protection Commissioner; the first, the legal scholar Hans Peter Bull, took office on 14 February 1978.
